content: The Union of Concerned Scientists (UCS) is a nonprofit advocacy organization headquartered in Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA. Its membership includes both professional scientists and private citizens. The UCS Board of Directors is chaired by Kurt Gottfried, a former senior staff member at CERN. The organization is also a member of the Sustainable Energy Coalition. The UCS advocates for increased Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards and supports measures to reduce smog pollution from construction equipment and diesel trucks. It endorses state laws aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles, modeled after California's regulations. The UCS calls for significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions in the United States and supports both national and international efforts to combat climate change. It has published reports detailing the regional effects of climate change within the United States. The organization supports a national renewable electricity standard, requiring utilities to generate a specific percentage of their energy from renewable sources such as wind, solar, and geothermal. While acknowledging that nuclear power can help reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the UCS maintains that nuclear energy must become significantly safer and more cost-effective before it can be considered a viable solution to global warming. The group advocates for stronger safety enforcement by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and other measures to improve nuclear power safety. The UCS monitors instances of political interference in science and supports whistleblower protections and free speech rights for federal scientists. Its scientific integrity program has conducted surveys of federal scientists across various agencies and issued a statement signed by over 11,000 scientists condemning political interference in science. The UCS advocates for reducing the use of antibiotics in livestock to prevent the development of antibiotic resistance in humans who consume treated animals. It opposes the cloning of animals for food and certain forms of genetic engineering. The organization also opposes the use of space weapons and supports the establishment of an international treaty to regulate military uses of space. Additionally, it works to reduce the global stockpile of nuclear weapons and opposes the Reliable Replacement Warhead program. The UCS has criticized the technical feasibility of missile defense systems and called for halting taxpayer-funded programs until they demonstrate the ability to address real-world threats. The UCS was founded in 1969 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) by faculty and students. One of its co-founders, physicist and Nobel laureate Dr. Henry Kendall, served as chairman of the UCS Board for many years. In 1977, the UCS sponsored a Scientists' Declaration on the Nuclear Arms Race, advocating for an end to nuclear weapons testing and deployment in the United States and the Soviet Union. In response to the Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI), the UCS sponsored a petition titled An Appeal to Ban Space Weapons. In 1992, Kendall presided over the UCS's Warning to Humanity, which called for fundamental changes to address a range of security and environmental issues. This document was signed by 1,700 scientists, including a majority of Nobel Prize winners in the sciences. Between 2000 and 2002, the UCS was the fourth-largest recipient of foundation grants for climate studies, with a quarter of its $24 million grant income allocated for that purpose. In 1997, the UCS circulated a petition titled A Call to Action, urging the ratification of the Kyoto Protocol. This petition was signed by 110 Nobel Prize laureates, including 104 Nobel-winning scientists. In February 2004, the UCS gained media attention for its publication Scientific Integrity in Policymaking, which criticized the administration of President George W. Bush for politicizing science. Allegations included altering information in global warming reports by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and selecting members of scientific advisory panels based on business interests rather than scientific expertise. In July 2004, the UCS released an addendum to the report, further criticizing the Bush administration for improperly altering reports on West Virginia strip mining and rejecting well-qualified nominees for government posts, such as Nobel laureate Torsten Wiesel, due to political differences. On April 2, 2004, Dr. John Marburger, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, issued a statement claiming that the UCS report contained false, incorrect, or distorted descriptions of incidents. Marburger dismissed the report as biased, while the UCS rebutted his claims, stating they were unjustified. The UCS later noted that the Bush administration had been largely silent on the issue since then. On October 15, 2005, in response to what it described as a changing political climate, the UCS announced the creation of a new Scientific Integrity Program to analyze and advocate for scientific integrity and against politically motivated interference. The UCS documented cases where officials at the U.S. Department of the Interior, including Deputy Assistant Secretary for Fish and Wildlife and Parks Julie MacDonald, systematically tampered with scientific data to undermine the protection of endangered species and the Endangered Species Act. On December 11, 2006, the UCS issued a statement signed by 10,600 leading scientists, including Nobel laureates, calling for the restoration of scientific integrity in federal policymaking. This announcement coincided with the group's efforts to document suspected censorship and political interference in federal science. On June 21, 2007, the UCS released a report documenting the political manipulation of scientific data to influence updated U.S. ozone regulations. Francesca Grifo, director of the UCS Scientific Integrity Program, stated, The law says use the science, the science says lower the standard to safe levels. She criticized the EPA for disregarding its own scientists' analysis, thereby risking the health of millions of Americans. The UCS has faced criticism from free-market advocacy groups and individuals for its positions on environmental and regulatory issues. Fred Singer, a University of Virginia professor and founder of the Science & Environmental Policy Project, has stated that the UCS has zero credibility as a scientific organization. The UCS has labeled Singer a climate contrarian and criticized his attempts to position himself as an objective, centrist, and apolitical figure.
